idiom_name: NewOrder(...) (*Order, error) constructor function with unexported fields
implementation_notes: Go has no constructors, so the factory is a package-level constructor function named NewT for type T that returns (*T, error), sets every field and leaves no valid-looking zero value to hand out; with unexported fields it is the only entry point from another package, because a composite literal naming those fields does not compile outside the package. What replaces the classic factory class is the package boundary itself; a factory struct or interface is justified only when creation must consult repositories or when several creation policies must be swappable, and functional options (WithCustomer(...)) are the idiomatic answer to many optional inputs.
pitfalls: Exported fields (or a literal written inside the same package) bypass NewOrder; every field whose value carries an invariant must stay unexported.
Returning a partially filled value together with a non-nil error invites misuse; return nil on failure and never let callers read the value when err != nil.
Go has no overloads, so give every creation path its own name (NewOrder, RehydrateOrder) instead of adding flag parameters that encode the path.
